## About this series
This series is adapted from my 2017 lecture notes, *Introduction to Statistical Tests* ([original PDF](/assets/docs/statests.pdf)). [Part 5](../stats-5-many-samples/index.qmd) compared several groups of measurements. Now we switch to **counts and proportions**.
:::

## When the data are counts

Not all data are measurements. Sometimes we count how many animals are healthy and how many are sick, how many voters say yes and how many say no, how many bacterial colonies are of one species or another. Such data are **counts in categories**, and the natural questions are about proportions: is the proportion of "yes" answers what we expect? Do two groups have the same proportion?

A large family of tests for this setting rests on the **$\chi^2$ statistic** (chi-squared). It compares the counts we *observed* in each category with those we would *expect* if the null hypothesis were true:

$$
\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{categories}} \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}.
$$

If observed and expected counts agree, every term is near zero. The more they disagree, the larger the statistic grows. What we need to turn it into a test is its distribution under $H_0$, and we can build that ourselves.

## Building the χ² distribution by simulation

Suppose a population of voters is split 50:50 between "yes" and "no". We poll 200 people, count the "yes" answers, compute $\chi^2$ against the expected 100 and 100, and then repeat the poll 10,000 times:

```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)

# A shared look for the figures in this series
accent <- "#8c2f39"; gold <- "#b08d4a"; ink <- "#5d6070"
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFDF8", colour = NA),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#EEEAE0", linewidth = 0.3),
          plot.title.position = "plot")
)
```

```{r simulate}
set.seed(6)
n <- 200
p_yes <- 0.5

yes  <- rbinom(10000, size = n, prob = p_yes)          # 10,000 polls of 200 people
chi2 <- (yes - n * p_yes)^2 / (n * p_yes) +             # "yes" cell
        ((n - yes) - n * (1 - p_yes))^2 / (n * (1 - p_yes))   # "no" cell

quantile(chi2, 0.95)      # the value exceeded in only 5% of polls
qchisq(0.95, df = 1)      # theory
```

```{r chi-plot}
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of simulated chi-squared values, heavily concentrated near zero with a long right tail, with the theoretical chi-squared density with one degree of freedom drawn over it and a vertical line at the 95th percentile."
ggplot(data.frame(chi2), aes(chi2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                 fill = "#d8cfba", colour = "#FFFDF8") +
  stat_function(fun = dchisq, args = list(df = 1), colour = accent, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = qchisq(0.95, 1), colour = gold, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8), ylim = c(0, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = expression(chi^2), y = "Density",
       title = "A simulated chi-squared distribution and the theoretical curve",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: the 95th percentile, 3.84")
```

Most simulated values are close to zero, as we would expect: the proportion in a sample usually lands close to the proportion in the population. A few polls come out far from 50:50, which gives the long right tail. The red curve is the theoretical $\chi^2$ distribution with **one degree of freedom** (two categories minus one), and the simulation agrees with it well. The simulated cutoff lands close to the theoretical 3.84. The histogram is a little uneven because, for a given number of respondents, the statistic can only take certain discrete values.

This gives us the recipe. Compute $\chi^2$ for the data, and if it exceeds the 95th percentile (3.84 for one degree of freedom) reject $H_0$, accepting that we will be wrong in 5% of the cases where $H_0$ is true. The degrees of freedom depend on the number of categories, and the right-hand tail area is the p-value.

## Testing one proportion

A Petri plate was left open in the main hall of the university for a while, then incubated for 40 hours at 37 °C. We counted 100 colonies of *Escherichia coli* and 30 of *Staphylococcus epidermidis*, so *S. epidermidis* makes up 30 of 130 colonies, about 23%. A reference study reports that it should account for 25% of the bacteria in such places. Is our plate consistent with that?

(We disregard all the usual complications: other bacteria that prefer different temperatures, no replicates, and so on.)

```{r prop-test}
prop.test(30, 130, p = 0.25)
```

`prop.test()` takes the number of "successes", the number of trials, and the hypothesised proportion. The p-value is large, so the plate gives no reason to doubt that the true share is 25%. The confidence interval is more informative: it says the true proportion could plausibly lie anywhere between about 16% and 31%. With so few colonies, the data are consistent with many values.

For small counts there is an **exact** alternative that does not rely on the $\chi^2$ approximation, the binomial test:

```{r binom}
binom.test(30, 130, p = 0.25)$p.value
```

The two agree here. The $\chi^2$ approximation is the one to avoid when expected counts are very small (a common rule of thumb says below 5 in any category).

## How precise is a poll?

Newspapers love exit polls. Suppose 55 of 100 people questioned say they will vote for a candidate. Does that mean the candidate wins?

```{r poll}
prop.test(55, 100)
```

The test of $H_0$: $p = 0.5$ has a large p-value, and the 95% confidence interval runs from about 45% to 65%. A lead of 5 percentage points in a sample of 100 is no lead at all. How does the width of the interval shrink as the sample grows? Keeping the observed share at 55%:

```{r poll-n}
n <- c(100, 400, 1000, 4000)
ci <- t(sapply(n, function(k) prop.test(round(0.55 * k), k)$conf.int))
data.frame(n = n, lower = round(ci[, 1], 3), upper = round(ci[, 2], 3),
           width = round(ci[, 2] - ci[, 1], 3))
```

The interval narrows only as the *square root* of the sample size: to halve it, you need four times as many respondents. For the 55% to be distinguishable from 50% we need a sample of roughly a thousand or more.

## What's next

We have tested a single proportion against a known value. In the next part we compare **several proportions**, check whether observed counts fit an expected distribution (is the die fair?), and test whether two categorical variables are independent.
